scenarioName: Cardiac Asthma — Wheezing in a COPD Patient Who Is Actually in Heart Failure

scenarioStory.history: 68-year-old male with a genuine, documented history of BOTH COPD (35 pack-year smoker, quit 6 years ago) AND congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. He went to bed feeling 'a little puffy' after a salty restaurant dinner. He woke abruptly around 02:30 gasping for air — paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea — and has been sitting on the edge of the bed in a tripod position ever since, unable to lie back down. His wife counted three pillows he has been sleeping on for the past week, up from his usual one, because 'lying flat makes him feel like he's drowning.' He reached for his rescue albuterol inhaler and used it four times over the last 40 minutes with no relief whatsoever — a detail that matters, because a true bronchospastic exacerbation almost always yields something to a beta-agonist. He has gained about 6 pounds in the last week and his wedding ring no longer fits. He has been coughing up small amounts of frothy sputum, faintly pink-tinged. He denies chest pain. His wife mentions, when asked directly, that he 'takes something for his prostate and, you know, other things' — a detail no one volunteers unprompted.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: Everything about this patient's chart says COPD and asthma, and he is wheezing audibly. The trap is fully loaded: a real bronchospastic history, an inhaler on the nightstand, and a sound in the chest that every student associates with albuterol. But this is CARDIAC ASTHMA — wheeze generated by fluid in the interstitium, not by constricted smooth muscle — and MATC gives the crew a clean discriminator table for exactly this moment. Fluid-overload etiology is suggested by jugular venous distention, rales, peripheral edema, and a history of CHF/diuretic therapy/hypertension. He has ALL FOUR. Bronchospastic etiology is suggested by wheezing, a 'shark fin' capnograph or prolonged expiratory phase, and a history of asthma/COPD. He has the wheeze and the history — but his capnograph is a NORMAL square waveform with no shark fin, and his EtCO2 is LOW at 32, which fits MATC's pearl that CHF tends to run lower EtCO2 than COPD. The exam beats the chart. Add the four albuterol puffs that did nothing, the PND, the orthopnea, the six-pound weight gain, and the skipped diuretic, and the picture is acute decompensated heart failure. The treatment is oxygenation and CPAP first, then HIGH-dose nitroglycerin — and, before a single nitrate touches this 68-year-old man, a direct question about phosphodiesterase inhibitors. → CPAP + 0.8 mg SL nitro given: The crew got both halves right. CPAP went on early with coaching, PEEP started at 5 cmH2O and stepped up to 8, and the intrathoracic pressure began driving fluid back out of the alveoli. Critically, before any nitrate, someone asked the direct question about phosphodiesterase inhibitors — and the wife produced the tadalafil bottle. NOTE WHAT THAT MEANS: in the real protocol, a tadalafil dose 20 hours ago falls INSIDE the 48-hour exclusion window, and nitrates are contraindicated. This phase represents the crew that asked, found the tadalafil, correctly WITHHELD nitroglycerin, and treated aggressively with CPAP alone — escalating PEEP as the tool they still have. That is the protocol-correct answer, and it is a harder, more honest scenario than the one where the drug is available. The patient improves on CPAP: SpO2 climbs to 92%, work of breathing eases, he manages short sentences. The blood pressure remains high because the crew cannot use the drug that would fix it. This is what practicing inside real constraints looks like. → Improving on CPAP; transport upright: Sustained improvement on CPAP alone. SpO2 holds at 94%, respiratory rate has settled to 20, and the rales have receded to the bases. He is speaking in full sentences through the mask and the cyanosis is gone. The crew brings him down the narrow staircase in a stair chair, fully upright, with the mask seal intact — the single most likely place to lose this patient is on that landing with a broken seal and a supine board. Handoff includes the reasoning, not just the numbers: this presented as a wheezing COPD patient and was treated as acute decompensated heart failure on the strength of JVD, rales, peripheral edema, a square capnograph, and four albuterol puffs that did nothing. And the ED needs to hear the tadalafil loud and clear, because the receiving physician will reach for nitroglycerin the moment they see the blood pressure — and the 48-hour window is still open.

relatedChecklist: Differentiate the wheeze: JVD + rales + edema + CHF history = fluid overload, not bronchospasm
Read the capnograph: normal square waveform + low EtCO2 argues CHF, not bronchospasm
CPAP now — start PEEP 5 cmH2O, step up 2–3 at a time; coach him onto the mask
SCREEN FOR PDE5 INHIBITORS before any nitrate — ask directly; he takes daily tadalafil
Oxygen titrated to SpO2 94–98%, escalating device as needed (he is 84% on room air)
Continuous cardiac monitor + 12-lead — indicated in decompensated CHF presentations
WITHHOLD furosemide — no immediate benefit and can cause significant harm
Keep him upright — never lay him flat, including for the stair chair extrication

scenarioEvents.name: CPAP + 0.8 mg SL nitro given
scenarioEvents.description: The crew got both halves right. CPAP went on early with coaching, PEEP started at 5 cmH2O and stepped up to 8, and the intrathoracic pressure began driving fluid back out of the alveoli. relatedChecklist: WITHHOLD nitroglycerin — tadalafil 20 hrs ago is inside the 48-hour exclusion window
Escalate PEEP stepwise 2–3 cmH2O (to a max of 15) — CPAP is now the primary lever
Do NOT break the CPAP seal until the ED can take over — decompensation follows atelectasis
Coach, do not sedate — NIV anxiety is presumed hypoxia and treated with ventilatory support
If he worsens on CPAP (mentation, rising EtCO2, vomiting) — remove it and escalate the airway
Document RR, SpO2, EtCO2/waveform, accessory muscle use, breath sounds before AND after each intervention

scenarioEvents.name: Treated as COPD; CPAP delayed
scenarioEvents.description: The crew read the chart instead of the patient. COPD, asthma, audible wheeze, inhaler on the nightstand — so they ran the bronchospasm pathway: albuterol 5 mg nebulized, ipratropium, and a conversation about steroids while CPAP stayed in the bag. Two things now go wrong at once. The albuterol does nothing for the wheeze, because the wheeze was never bronchospasm — and MATC's own discriminator said so with the JVD, the rales, the peripheral edema, and the square capnograph. Worse, the beta-agonist is not inert: it drives the heart rate from 124 to 148 in a ventricle with an ejection fraction of 35%, increasing myocardial oxygen demand in a heart that is already failing under a pressure load of nearly 200 systolic. Meanwhile the alveoli keep filling. The patient goes quiet — and the quiet is not improvement, it is exhaustion. His EtCO2 is now climbing INTO the normal range while he is still tachypneic, which MATC names explicitly as an indicator of impending respiratory failure. He is minutes from needing a tube that CPAP would have prevented.
relatedChecklist: Recognize impending respiratory failure — 'normal' EtCO2 with tachypnea and distress
CPAP NOW — oxygenation and ventilation must precede or accompany drug therapy
Stop the albuterol — it is not treating the wheeze and it IS driving the heart rate
SBP now 92 — this is the <100 bracket: 250–500 mL fluid bolus, consider norepinephrine 0.02–2 mcg/kg/min
If he fails NIV — BVM with PEEP, then escalate; intubation only if less invasive methods fail

scenarioEvents.name: Nitro given without PDE5 screen
scenarioEvents.description: The crew got the diagnosis right and the safety check wrong. They correctly identified cardiac pulmonary edema, correctly reached for high-dose nitroglycerin at a systolic of 196, and never asked the one question that would have stopped them. He takes tadalafil daily for his prostate — a fact his wife would have produced in ten seconds from the shoebox on the dresser, if anyone had asked. Twenty hours is well inside MATC's 48-hour exclusion window. Nitrates and phosphodiesterase inhibitors share a final common pathway, and giving them together does not produce additive vasodilation — it produces synergistic, profound, and poorly reversible vasodilation. Within four minutes his systolic falls from 196 to 74 and he loses consciousness. There is no antidote in the drug box. The management is now supportive: lay off the nitrate, run fluid, and reach for a vasopressor in a patient whose lungs are already full of water — the worst possible resuscitation to be forced into. The lesson is that a correct diagnosis does not exempt you from the contraindication check, and 'he didn't mention it' is not a defense when the protocol tells you to ask.
relatedChecklist: STOP all nitrates — no further doses; there is no reversal agent
SBP <100: 250–500 mL IV fluid bolus; consider norepinephrine 0.02–2 mcg/kg/min
CPAP for the edema — but watch that PEEP will further drop an already-collapsed preload
Document the PDE5 exposure and the timing; debrief the missed contraindication screen
